newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss telecoms reorganisation clears next hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Swiss telecoms reorganisation clears next hurdle.

text.p: Switzerland's upper house of parliament on Thursday approved a package of legislation that will overhaul the post office and partially privatise telecommunications in 1998.

The package, approved in December by the lower house in Berne, aims to split the state Post, Telephone and Telegraph authority (PTT) into two seperate units. Minor differences in the two houses' versions must still be worked out.
A Telecom PTT spokesman in Berne said he hoped the reforms could win final legislative approval by the end of the current session on March 21, but added they may be delayed until June.
In any event, opponents of the reforms could force a referendum on the package under Switzerland's system of direct democracy. This could delay the process up to two years.

Telecommunications activities will be transformed into a joint stock company, with the Swiss government holding a majority. The postal authority will remain a state-owned agency without benefit of cross-subsidy from the telecoms arm.
The goal is to sell a minority stake in Swiss Telecom so that the company could be listed in the second half of 1998.
Full privatisation is not envisaged because this would require changing the Swiss constitution, a lengthy process.
The reform is scheduled to take effect on January 1, 1998, in line with the European Union's liberalisation of its telecommuncations market.

Switzerland took a first step to loosening its telecommunications law in 1991, letting private companies offer some kinds of data transmission. But the PTT still holds a monopoly over most voice transmission and the cellular network.
Switzerland's place in the top 10 telecommunications markets and its fat margins should attract several competitors when the telecoms monoply falls in 1998, to the joy of consumers.

But privatisation plans have been viewed with suspicion for years by politicians who fear some customers in remote areas could lose their telephone service. Unions representing 46,000 postal and Telecom workers also oppose the reforms.
Telecom PTT is required to provide general basic service for five years after the changes come in. New competitors can offer regional service.
But the PTT is girding to compete. It has lured away a top executive from IBM Europe to run its telecoms operations and has started investing in foreign markets.
Swiss Telecom took restructuring charges of 681 million Swiss francs in 1996, cutting net profit fell to 746 million from 1.43 billion in 1995. Profit before charges was steady.
In addition to restructuring charges, it took extraordinary write-offs of 482 million last year. Cash flow was 3.9 billion.
